awd_titl_txt: General Cognitive Diagnosis Models: Development, Estimation, and Applications
awd_abstract_narration:
This research project will advance the frontiers of modern statistical theory and methodology in cognitive diagnosis modeling. Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) are psychometric tools designed to infer respondents' unobserved psychological attributes from their manifest responses to a set of items in a test or questionnaire. CDMs have been used in educational assessments and successfully applied in psychology and the social sciences. However, existing CDMs have limited utility because they often assume binary attributes. This project will further extend the applicability of CDMs by developing a general family of models that offer a unified framework for CDM analyses, and that also can be used as a basis for the development of new CDMs. The scientific products of this project will be disseminated via workshops, conference presentations, and publications in peer-reviewed journals. The project will develop open-source software to make advanced CDMs accessible to a broader audience. The outcomes of this project will be useful for applied researchers in education, psychology, and the social sciences. Both undergraduate and graduate students will be involved in the conduct of this research, and the investigators will make every effort to include students of underrepresented groups in their research teams.
 
This research project will develop, estimate, and apply a novel family of cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) to simultaneously accommodate polytomous response data and multi-categorical psychological attributes. In particular, the project will (1) examine the theoretical properties of the proposed models, including model identifiability and model equivalence to ensure the principled use of CDMs in practice, (2) develop computationally efficient parameter estimation methods to make it possible to estimate parameters of CDMs of high dimensions in big data, (3) develop valid statistical inference methods for handling models of high dimensions and data of large sizes, and (4) conduct interdisciplinary collaborations to apply the new methods to representative datasets in various scientific fields to address substantive research questions of interest. To boost the impact of the proposed work, the investigators will create a free software program to make the methodological innovations accessible to applied researchers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This research project addresses key challenges in the practical application of confirmatory cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs), including the analysis of polytomous response data, the modeling of polytomous attributes, the parameter estimation under high dimensionality, and the identifiability of parameters. CDMs provide a foundation for developing diagnostic assessments that characterize individuals’ strengths and areas for improvement in education, psychology, and other social and behavioral sciences. The project extends these models to accommodate diverse assessment settings and advances parameter estimation in high-dimensional contexts. It also establishes identifiability conditions for the newly developed models, providing a theoretical foundation for recovering model parameters from observed data. Through interdisciplinary collaborations, the project evaluates the applicability and utility of CDMs across fields. Complementing these methodological and theoretical contributions, the project develops R tools to make the methods accessible to practitioners and applied researchers.

The research findings have been widely disseminated to relevant scholarly and professional communities. The project has produced multiple publications in leading psychometrics and statistics journals, such as Applied Psychological Measurement, Behavior Research Methods, Behaviormetrika, British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, Journal of Educational Measurement, and Psychometrika. The research team has also presented its findings at national conferences, including the annual meetings of the American Educational Research Association and the National Council on Measurement in Education. Software and supporting code have been distributed through the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) and the Open Science Framework (OSF), supporting broader access, reproducibility, and adoption of the proposed methods.

The project has also provided opportunities for mentorship and student training. Both principal investigators have advised doctoral and undergraduate students at the University of Minnesota and the University of Michigan through project-related research activities. These activities offer students experience in methodological research, statistical computing, and interdisciplinary collaboration, helping prepare them for future work in quantitative research and applied measurement.

From a societal perspective, the models and methods developed through this project have substantial potential to expand the use of diagnostic assessments in education, psychology, and related fields. In particular, the findings could support the development of tools that identify specific learning challenges and skill gaps among students in STEM. Such tools could provide a foundation for targeted instructional support, individualized feedback, and remediation informed by students’ diagnostic profiles. By strengthening both the theoretical foundations and practical accessibility of CDMs, the project supports more informative assessment and better-informed educational decisions.
